attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter. Pro example echoes Altman, but the universal claim is his.

semantics.note: Faithful present-tense observation: every transaction loses money, Pro included.

contract.note: The plain reading (revenue per transaction fails to cover attributable cost) is ordinary. Using January 2025 up to the post date is a fair window. Treating Pro as a product-level loss is fair.

evidence.note: Altman's Jan 6, 2025 post is a company disclosure that Pro subscriptions collectively lost money. It backs only the narrower Pro example, not every transaction.
Estimate of API gross margin for June 2024. It covers a different period and basis (gross, GPU-only) and is acknowledged as unverified, so it cannot contradict the January 2025 claim.

reviews.rationale: A company disclosure confirms Pro lost money in aggregate, but there is no January 2025 transaction-level revenue and cost evidence for the universal claim that every transaction lost money. The API margin estimate is for an earlier period and a different basis. Neither support nor contradiction is established.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his newsletter.

semantics.note: "It's going to be a hard sell" is unhedged, so this is a scored forecast. No deadline is given. The NVIDIA aside is rightly left out.

contract.note: Reading it as material investor resistance tied to DeepSeek economics is ordinary and fair. Results depend on how severe a 'hard sell' must be and on separating GPU spending from total capex; the speaker set neither.

evidence.note: Reuters, Feb 2025: investor unease and executives defending AI spending after DeepSeek. The selloff is also tied to slowing cloud growth, so it does not isolate resistance driven by DeepSeek.
Alphabet's Q2 2025 capex of $22.4B is total capex, not GPU spending or market acceptance. It is not conclusive either way.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, and no dated event meets the early-resolution rule. Investor concern and continued capex are both mixed with other factors and do not isolate GPU spending or DeepSeek's role. The forecast cannot be scored yet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the three burdens and 'necessary costs'. But it asserts that the bubble was inflated because of a premise, and it rejects a necessity claim. Both are causal, so labelling it an observation misfits; the contract's causal axis is right.

contract.note: Requiring a premise that drove investment plus a counterexample showing the burdens were unnecessary follows his words. The demands on grid and emissions evidence are strict but tied to what he wrote.

evidence.note: Explains that the $5.6M figure covers only the final training run and leaves out prior research and hardware. This limits the counterexample but does not settle necessity.
TIME, Jan 2025: efficiency may cut projected emissions, but the outcome is uncertain. No measured grid or emissions-goal data.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet shows the necessity premise drove the whole investment boom. Nothing documents a competitive model's full costs, grid impact, or emissions-goal performance. The evidence leaves both the causal claim and the necessity claim unsettled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Faithful to the profitability part. The 'transformer has peaked' clause is rightly split off as a separate claim.

contract.note: Drawing 2024 from the surrounding loss figures and reading 'unsustainable' as reliance on outside funding are ordinary readings. 'In 2024' is contextual, not in the sentence itself. The result depends on how LLM services are separated from the rest of each company.

evidence.note: Projected 2024 company-wide loss for OpenAI, not a realized result; CNBC had not seen the accounts. It suggests OpenAI loses money but covers one company only.
Alphabet keeps general AI model costs unallocated and does not isolate LLM profit or loss.
Meta's segments do not separate LLM revenue and costs.

reviews.rationale: The only evidence pointing toward losses is a projected company-wide OpenAI figure. There is no Anthropic data, and Google's and Meta's disclosures do not isolate LLM economics. Nothing establishes 2024 losses and outside-funding dependence across all four, and nothing shows any of them was profitable.
